candidates.title: King Ocean consolidates Haiti services, reduces Cap-Haïtien calls
candidates.excerpt: King Ocean Services has consolidated its two weekly container shipping services between Port Everglades in Florida and Haiti into a single rotation, reducing the number of vessels deployed on the trade from two to one. Under the revised arrangement, Port-au-Prince will retain its weekly connection with Port Everglades, while calls at Cap-Haïtien will be reduced to a fortnightly frequency. The new port rotation will be: Port Everglades – Port-au-Prince – Cap-Haïtien (fortnightly) – Port Everglades. The consolidation represents a reduction in the carrier’s vessel deployment on the Haiti trade, combining the previously separate weekly connections into one service covering both Haitian ports. While Port-au-Prince will continue receiving weekly calls, the revised schedule will halve the frequency of direct calls at Cap-Haïtien, changing the availability of regular shipping connections for cargo moving through the northern Haitian port. candidates.title: From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping
candidates.excerpt: From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida, to become what is expected to be the world’s largest artificial reef. Initial underwater inspections found the vessel upright, approximately 180 feet below the surface. The sinking of the SS United States reminds us that ships can outlive their commercial purpose. Launched in 1951 and entering service in 1952, the SS United States was the pinnacle of post-war American maritime engineering. It held the record as the world’s fastest passenger ship but was withdrawn in 1969 as commercial aviation transformed the economics of transatlantic travel. candidates.title: New report identifies Hong Kong’s place in world shipping
candidates.excerpt: New report identifies Hong Kong’s place in world shipping Hong Kong Maritime Week is about to kick off. To celebrate the occasion, Splash today publishes a 48-page magazine on the city’s maritime hub credentials. A ship can be ordered at a mainland Chinese yard, owned through a leasing company in Hong Kong, insured in London, crewed through a management operation in Asia and chartered from Singapore. Its cargo need never pass through Hong Kong’s harbour. Even its Hong Kong financing vehicle may have to seek credit approval elsewhere. The geography of shipping has always been complicated. What has changed is the urgency with which Hong Kong must ask where the real business takes place. Is the city still a maritime capital in its own right, chosen by international owners, traders and financiers because of what it offers? candidates.excerpt: Genesee & Wyoming Inc. is planning to separate into three rail holding companies, effective Jan. 1, 2027, a move that will position the regional entities for eventual sale. The companies will continue to be owned by G&W parent Brookfield and GIC. G&W operates more than 100 railroads. The new companies are: Atlantic & Great Lakes Transportation Inc., which will be made up of G&W operations in New England (including Berkshire & Eastern Railroad), New York, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. Atlantic & Great Lakes will be based in Rochester, N.Y., and led by Chief Executive Bill Keough, who has been with G&W for eight years and most recently served as regional senior vice president. Canyon & Cascade Transportation Inc., which will be comprised of G&W operations in Washington, Oregon, California, Arizona, and New Mexico. candidates.title: Intermodal leads U.S. rail traffic up 6.6% from a year ago
candidates.excerpt: Rail traffic among U.S. carriers rose 6.6% in the week ending Nov. 7 compared with the same week a year ago, driven by an 11% increase in intermodal shipments, the Association of American Railroads said. Carloads increased 1.3% from a year earlier. Seven of the 10 commodity groups recorded gains, led by motor vehicles and parts, up 10.4%, and forest products, up 10.1%. Metallic ores and metals followed with a 6.4% increase. Grain shipments declined 2.4%, nonmetallic minerals fell 1.7%, and coal slipped 1.2% among weaker volumes. Through the first 44 weeks of 2026, total U.S. rail traffic increased 3.9% compared with the same period in 2025. Intermodal volume rose 4.9%, carloads increased 2.7%. Grain remained the strongest-growing freight category year to date, up 9.7%, despite its weekly decline. Metallic ores and metals increased 8.8%, and petroleum and petroleum products rose 7.7%. US rail traffic hits intermodal record as October freight gains signal economic resilience, says AAR
candidates.excerpt: U.S. railroads set an intermodal traffic record in October as shipments rose across much of the freight economy, evidence of resilient demand despite inflation, higher interest rates and weak consumer confidence. Intermodal volume rose 9.6% from a year earlier, with railroads handling an average of more than 298,000 containers and trailers per week — the highest weekly average for any month on record, according to the Association of American Railroads. Total carloads increased 3.4%, their strongest percentage gain in eight months, while carloads excluding coal climbed 4.5%. Fifteen of the 20 carload categories tracked by the AAR posted year-over-year increases in October, and 16 were higher through the first 10 months of 2026. The association said that breadth pointed to underlying industrial strength rather than simply a shift of freight from highways to rail.
